newsitem.title: HONG KONG: AMR's services unit tapping Asian market.
newsitem.headline: AMR's services unit tapping Asian market.

text.p: AMR Corp's aviation services division AMR Airline Services said on Tuesday it aimed to tap the growing Asian market, seeking business in the development and management of new terminals and airports.
"The region is experiencing extraordinary growth in air transport demand, with a related need for airport infrastructure development," president Bella Goren told a news conference.
"Countries such as China, the Philippines, Indonesia, Australia and India offer particularly great potential," she said.

"In addition to our traditional passenger and ramp services, cargo, fueling and maintenance services, AMR Services will also offer broad-guage services such as management and development of airport passenger and cargo terminals, management and operation of privatised airport companies as well as airport and terminal BOT (build-operate-transfer) projects," she said.
Barry Nassberg, assistant vice president Asia and Eastern Europe, said terminal development and terminal management was an area the company hoped to focus on in China.
The firm was in talks on projects in China and the rest of the region, he said, but declined to elaborate.
The company set up an office in Hong Kong last month as its headquarters for the region.

On Tuesday, it signed with the territory's Airport Authority a 10-year into-plane fuelling services franchise at the new Hong Kong airport at Chek Lap Kok, a contract valued at US$60 million in revenue over the contract period.
Nassberg said investment in the project would be about US$10 million, of which most would be forked out initially although a portion would be injected in subsequent years.
Funds would come from AMR Corp's financial resources, he said.
The firm's service charges at Chek Lap Kok would be competitive, similar to if not lower than the current rates at Hong Kong's existing Kai Tak Airport, Nassberg said.
But the final price structure had to be finalised, he added.
Goren said she expected to have about 50 employees to work for the fuelling project.
The group is a member of a consortium proposing to operate the general aviation terminal at Chek Lap Kok, she noted.
